5.3.1:
Why this matters

Every control costs something: inspection time, audits, training, monitoring software, calibration. A project that adds expensive controls everywhere can eat its own savings. Cost-benefit analysis decides which controls are worth keeping, and proves that the project's gains are protected at a sensible cost.

The big idea

Controls exist to prevent regression: the process sliding back to its old performance. So the question is:

Is the cost of sustaining this control less than the expected cost of losing the improvement without it?

  • Cost of the control: setup (one-time) plus ongoing costs: people's time for checks and audits, data collection, equipment, training, maintenance.
  • Benefit of the control: the savings it protects (hard and soft, 1.3.3), multiplied by how likely regression would be without it.

Worked example

A project cut damage claims from $480,000 to $200,000 a year, saving $280,000. Proposed controls:

ControlAnnual cost
Weekly load-securing audits$15,000
Annual driver refresher training$10,000
Monthly claims p chart and review$3,000
Total$28,000

Without controls, the team estimates half the gain would erode within a year: $140,000 at risk. Spending $28,000 a year to protect $140,000 (or more) is clearly justified: the expected net benefit is $112,000 a year.

If a further control (say, cameras on every dock at $150,000 a year) would only protect an extra $20,000, it is not justified.

Using ROI and payback

The same tools as project selection (1.3.3) apply:

  • ROI = (benefit − cost) ÷ cost.
  • Payback = investment ÷ annual net benefit.

Include ongoing costs, which are easy to forget, and both hard and soft benefits (the soft ones, such as customer retention, can be decisive even when hard numbers are close).

Choosing the cheapest effective control

Controls range from cheap to expensive, and strong to weak. Prefer, roughly in this order:

  1. Mistake-proofing (5.1.3): built in, little ongoing cost, very strong.
  2. Standard work, visual controls and training: low cost, moderately strong.
  3. SPC monitoring: moderate cost, catches drift early.
  4. Inspection and audits: ongoing labor cost, catches problems after the fact.

Check yourself

  1. What does a control protect against?
  2. A control costs $50,000 a year and protects an expected $30,000 of savings. Justified?
  3. Name two ongoing costs of a control.
  4. Why is mistake-proofing often the best-value control?
Show answers
  1. Regression: the process sliding back to its old performance.
  2. Not on these numbers (cost exceeds the protected benefit), unless important soft benefits or risks justify it.
  3. Any two of: audit time, data collection, training, monitoring software, calibration, maintenance.
  4. It is strong (prevents the error) and usually has low ongoing cost once installed.

Key takeaways

  • Compare the cost of sustaining a control with the benefit it protects.
  • Use ROI and payback, including ongoing costs and soft benefits.
  • Prefer strong, low-cost controls: mistake-proofing first, inspection last.
5.3.2:
Why this matters

When the project team hands over, the gains depend on the people who run the process every day. The control plan is the document that tells them exactly what to watch, how, how often, and what to do if something goes wrong. Without it, improvements fade.

The big idea

A control plan is a table (one row per controlled characteristic) that documents how the process will be kept in its improved state. It is the main Control-phase deliverable and is handed to the process owner.

The columns

ElementWhat it saysExample
Process stepWhere in the processLoad securing
Characteristic (CTQ or critical X)What is controlled: an output (Y) or a key input (X)Strap tension; claims per 1,000 loads
Specification / targetThe requirementAt least 4 straps per 10 ft of freight
Measurement methodHow it is measured (with a capable measurement system, 2.3)Visual check with photo; claims system report
Sample sizeHow many5 trailers per shift
FrequencyHow oftenEvery shift; monthly for claims
Control methodThe tool usedChecklist and photo; p chart of claims
Owner (who)Who does itDock lead; terminal manager
Reaction planWhat to do if out of control or out of specSee response plan R-07
Document referenceWhere the procedure livesSOP-LS-03

Remember monitor the Y, control the X's (1.1.4): control plans usually include the critical X's that drive the result, not only the output.

Supporting items

  • Standard operating procedures (SOPs) and work instructions updated to the new method.
  • Training records: everyone doing the work trained on the new method.
  • Process owner named and accepting responsibility.
  • Transition plan: how and when the project team hands over (often with a period of joint monitoring).

A living document

The control plan belongs to the process owner, not the project team, and it is updated whenever the process, specifications or measurement methods change. It should match the current FMEA (2.1.4): the high-risk failure modes in the FMEA should have controls in the plan.

Worked example: what is wrong?

A control plan row reads: "Claims per 1,000 loads; target under 1.5; p chart; monthly." What is missing?

  • No owner: who reviews the chart?
  • No reaction plan: what happens if the chart signals?
  • No measurement method or sample size details, and no document reference.

A plan without an owner and a reaction plan is the most common weakness: the data gets collected and nobody acts on it.

Check yourself

  1. Who owns the control plan after the project closes?
  2. Name five columns of a control plan.
  3. A control plan lists what to measure and how often, but not what to do when a problem appears. What is missing?
  4. Why should a control plan include critical X's, not just the Y?
Show answers
  1. The process owner.
  2. Any five of: process step, characteristic, specification/target, measurement method, sample size, frequency, control method, owner, reaction plan, document reference.
  3. The reaction plan.
  4. Controlling the inputs prevents problems; watching only the output finds them after they happen.

Key takeaways

  • The control plan documents how gains are held: step, characteristic, spec, measurement, sample size, frequency, control method, owner, reaction plan, document reference.
  • Supported by SOPs, training, a named process owner and a transition plan.
  • A living document owned by the process owner, aligned with the FMEA.
5.3.3:
Why this matters

Detecting a problem is only half of control. The response plan (reaction plan) makes sure that when a chart signals or a product fails specification, people act quickly, correctly and consistently, instead of improvising, ignoring it, or tampering.

The big idea

A response plan is a pre-agreed set of steps, written before problems happen, that says: when this trigger occurs, who does what, in what order, and when to escalate.

The elements

  1. Trigger: the exact condition that starts the plan. An out-of-control signal (which rules, 5.2.10), an out-of-spec result, an audit failure.
  2. Immediate containment: stop the damage. Hold suspect product, stop the process if needed, segregate affected loads, notify the next step or the customer.
  3. Who acts: the named person responsible for each step, and their authority (for example, the operator may stop the line).
  4. Investigation: find the special cause. What changed? Use quick tools: 5 Whys, checking recent changes, stratifying the data.
  5. Corrective action: fix the cause, and prevent recurrence (update the FMEA, mistake-proof if possible).
  6. Escalation: when to involve the supervisor, the process owner, quality or management (for example, if not resolved within 2 hours, or if the customer is affected).
  7. Documentation: record what happened, the cause found and the action taken (on the chart and in a log), so patterns become visible over time.
  8. Resume: the criteria for restarting normal operation and releasing held product.

Product disposition

For out-of-spec product, the plan states the decision rules: use as is (with approval), rework, sort and inspect, return to supplier, or scrap, and who may decide.

Out of control vs out of spec

These are different situations and need different responses:

SituationMeaningResponse
Out of control, within specA special cause has appeared, though product still meets requirementsInvestigate and remove the special cause before it causes defects
In control, out of specThe stable process is not capableNo special cause to find; contain product and improve the system (reduce variation or recenter, a project)
Out of control and out of specA special cause is producing defectsContain product immediately, investigate, correct
In control and within specNormalLeave it alone (no tampering)

Worked example

A p chart of late deliveries shows a point above the UCL on Tuesday.

  1. Trigger: point beyond UCL (rule 1).
  2. Contain: dispatch reviews Wednesday's at-risk loads and calls affected customers.
  3. Investigate (dispatch supervisor): Tuesday's data show most late loads came from one terminal, where a dock door was out of service.
  4. Correct: reroute loads while the door is repaired; add dock-door status to the morning huddle.
  5. Escalate: not needed (resolved within the day).
  6. Document: annotate the chart ("Dock door 4 down") and log the incident.
  7. Resume: normal operation once the door is repaired and the next day's rate is back within limits.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • After an out-of-control signal: contain, investigate, correct, document. Not "adjust and move on", and not "recalculate the limits".
  • Out of control is not the same as out of spec.
  • A response plan names who acts and when to escalate.
  • Stable but out of spec needs a system change, not a hunt for a special cause.

Check yourself

  1. List the main steps after an out-of-control signal.
  2. A stable process makes some out-of-spec parts. Is there a special cause to investigate?
  3. Why should a response plan be written before problems occur?
  4. What is containment?
  5. A point is out of control but the product is within spec. Should anything be done?
Show answers
  1. Contain, investigate, correct (and prevent recurrence), escalate if needed, document, resume.
  2. No. The process is stable; the problem is the system (capability). Contain product and improve the process.
  3. So the response is fast, consistent and correct under pressure, with clear ownership.
  4. Immediate action to stop the problem spreading: holding suspect product, stopping the process, notifying those affected.
  5. Yes. Investigate the special cause before it produces defects.

Key takeaways

  • Response plan: trigger, containment, who acts, investigation, corrective action, escalation, documentation, resume.
  • Includes disposition rules for out-of-spec product.
  • Out of control ≠ out of spec: investigate special causes; improve the system for capability problems.
